# 2 Samuel Chapter 3 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 170v–172r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_003_page_001.jpg, 2SA_003_page_002.jpg, 2SA_003_page_003.jpg

---

**1** The war between the house of Saul and the house of David dragged on. David grew stronger and stronger, while Saul's house grew weaker and weaker.

**2** Sons were born to David in Hebron: his firstborn Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel; **3** his second, Chileab, by Abigail, Nabal's widow from Carmel; the third, Absalom, whose mother was Maacah daughter of King Talmai of Geshur; **4** the fourth, Adonijah, son of Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah, son of Abital; **5** and the sixth, Ithream, by David's wife Eglah. These were born to David in Hebron.

**6** During the war between the two houses, Abner was consolidating his own power within Saul's house.

**7** Now Saul had had a concubine named Rizpah daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth confronted Abner: "Why have you slept with my father's concubine?"

**8** Abner exploded with rage. "Am I some Judean dog's head? I have been faithful to your father Saul's house — to his family and his allies — and I haven't handed you over to David! And now you charge me with a crime over a woman?

**9** May God strike me dead and worse if I don't do for David exactly what the LORD swore to him — **10** transferring the kingdom from Saul's house and establishing David's throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba!"

**11** Ish-bosheth could not say another word to Abner. He was too afraid of him.

**12** Abner sent envoys to David immediately: "Whose land is this, really? Make a deal with me, and I will bring all Israel to your side."

**13** "Good," David replied. "I will make a deal with you. But I have one condition: do not come to see me unless you bring Michal, Saul's daughter, with you."

**14** David also sent word to Ish-bosheth: "Give me back my wife Michal, whom I won for the price of a hundred Philistine foreskins."

**15** Ish-bosheth sent for her and took her away from her husband Paltiel son of Laish. **16** Her husband walked behind her, weeping all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner told him, "Go home." And he turned back.

**17** Abner had already been working the elders of Israel: "You've wanted David as your king for a long time now. **18** So make it happen — the LORD himself said about David: 'Through my servant David I will deliver my people Israel from the Philistines and from all their enemies.'"

**19** Abner also spoke privately with the Benjaminites. Then he went to Hebron to tell David everything that Israel and the whole tribe of Benjamin were ready to support.

**20** When Abner arrived in Hebron with twenty men, David threw a feast for them.

**21** Abner said to David, "Let me go now and rally all Israel for my lord the king. They will make a covenant with you, and you will rule over everything your heart desires." David sent Abner off in peace.

**22** Just then Joab and David's men returned from a raid, loaded with plunder. Abner was already gone — David had sent him away in peace. **23** When Joab arrived and was told, "Abner son of Ner came to the king, and the king let him go in peace," **24** Joab stormed in to the king: "What have you done? Abner comes to you and you just let him walk out? **25** You know Abner son of Ner! He came to spy on you — to track your movements and find out everything you're doing."

**26** Joab left David and sent messengers after Abner, who brought him back from the cistern of Sirah. David knew nothing about it.

**27** When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab pulled him aside into the gateway, as if to speak privately. There he stabbed him in the belly, and Abner died — payment for the blood of Asahel, Joab's brother.

**28** When David heard about it afterward, he declared, "I and my kingdom are completely innocent before the LORD of the blood of Abner son of Ner!

**29** Let it come crashing down on the head of Joab and on his whole family! May the house of Joab never be without someone suffering from a running sore, or skin disease, or who is crippled, or who dies by the sword, or who goes hungry!"

**30** Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel at the battle of Gibeon.

**31** David ordered Joab and everyone with him: "Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and walk in mourning ahead of Abner's body." King David himself walked behind the bier.

**32** They buried Abner in Hebron. The king broke down and wept at Abner's grave, and all the people wept with him.

**33** The king sang this lament over Abner:
"Should Abner have died like some senseless fool?

**34** Your hands were never bound.
Your feet were never shackled.
You fell the way a man falls before criminals."
The people broke down weeping over him again.

**35** They all came urging David to eat while it was still daylight, but David swore an oath: "May God strike me dead if I taste bread or anything else before the sun goes down!"

**36** Everyone saw it and approved — as they approved everything the king did.

**37** That day all the people and all Israel understood that the king had had no part in killing Abner son of Ner.

**38** The king said to his officials, "Don't you realize that a commander and a great man has fallen today in Israel?

**39** I may be the anointed king, but today I am powerless. These sons of Zeruiah — they are too ruthless for me. May the LORD repay the one who does evil according to his evil."

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 6 — "consolidating his own power":** The Hebrew *mitchazzeq* (hithpael of *chazaq*) means "was making himself strong" — a reflexive verb suggesting self-serving political maneuvering. Abner was building his own base within the failing monarchy.

**Verse 8 — "Judean dog's head":** The Hebrew is compressed and explosive. The meaning seems to be: "Am I a worthless dog loyal to Judah?" — i.e., "Do you think I'm secretly working for David?" Abner's fury reveals how fragile the power structure really is.

**Verse 16 — "weeping all the way":** This is one of the most heartbreaking moments in the whole narrative. Paltiel is given no words — just tears. He is a man losing his wife to a political power play, and the narrator lets his silent grief speak for itself. The Hebrew *halokh u-vakho* (going and weeping) uses the continuous participle — the weeping never stops until Abner orders him to turn back.

**Verse 27 — "as if to speak privately":** The Hebrew *ba-sheli* (in quietness/secrecy) is devastating. Joab uses the language of private diplomacy to commit murder. The location — the gateway, the threshold between safety and danger — is symbolically charged. And the wound is in the *chomesh*, the belly — the same spot where Abner killed Asahel. The blood-vengeance cycle completes itself with surgical precision.

**Verse 33 — "senseless fool":** Hebrew *naval*. David is asking: was this a death worthy of Abner? The answer is no — a bound prisoner might die helplessly, but Abner was free, unshackled, walking in peace under royal guarantee. He was murdered through treachery, not overcome in battle. The word *naval* also invokes Nabal from 1 Samuel 25 — a man whose name meant "fool" and who died a senseless death.

**Verse 39 — "too ruthless for me":** David's admission is extraordinary. The anointed king confesses that Joab's family is beyond his control — *qashim mimmenni*, literally "harder/harsher than me." This is a king acknowledging a power vacuum in his own court, and it foreshadows the unresolved tension with Joab that will persist until David's deathbed charge to Solomon (1 Kings 2).

*— PNEUMA*
